summary: Defines the Group Security Policy Token, a structure that spells out the security policy and settings for a cryptographic group such as a secure multicast group. Because group security depends on many services working together, an authenticatable description of what every part of the system must support helps keep them consistent. This is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: A club has house rules written on a card that is signed so nobody can fake it. Everyone who joins reads the same card and follows the same rules, so the whole club stays safe together.

subtitle: A signed, ASN.1-encoded rulebook that tells every member of a secure multicast group which security mechanisms the group uses.

tldr.problem: Security for a group such as a secure multicast group depends on many services and mechanisms working together, so everyone needs an authenticatable statement of what the whole system must support.
tldr.mechanism: The Group Security Policy Token is an ASN.1 structure, DER encoded and signed by the Group Owner with a CMS SignedData wrapper. It lists the registration, rekey and data protocols and their parameters.
tldr.outcome: A group member or controller can check who wrote the policy, that it is newer than the last one, and that its own local policy supports the listed mechanisms before joining. The group is only as strong as the weakest mechanism the Group Owner accepts.

today: RFC 4534 is a Proposed Standard from June 2006. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of version 1 of the token.

sections.title: Why a Policy Token
sections.content:
The Multicast Group Security Architecture defines the infrastructure for secure group communication. The policy token assumes that architecture and defines the enforceable security parameters for a Group Secure Association.

The token is signed by the Group Owner, the entity with authority to create security policy. Group controllers use it to check that the mechanisms securing the group are correct and to enforce the rules for joining members. Members use it to confirm that the group is owned by a trusted authority, and may also check that the access rules are adequate for the data they submit.

The token is written in ASN.1 and DER encoded, so it can describe groups that span different applications and environments. Any group can use it to name several protocols for securing the group.
sections.eli5: The token is the group's rule card. The person in charge signs it, so members know the rules are real and the group controllers know which rules to enforce.

sections.title: A Core Token with Pluggable Mechanisms
sections.content:
The design keeps the core token small and pushes detail into replaceable parts. It does this with a generic construct pairing an OBJECT IDENTIFIER with an OCTET STRING of parameters, which lets mechanisms defined in other documents be used with the token.

The token follows the layers of the MSEC architecture. Each layer gets its own branch in the core token. New protocols at any layer can therefore be added without changing the core token, which acts as a single point of reference for defining secure groups using any mix of protocols.

The RFC says protocols beyond registration, rekey and data SHOULD NOT be added to later versions unless the MSEC architecture changes.
sections.eli5: The rule card has fixed boxes to fill in, and each box can point to a different rulebook. New rulebooks can be added without redesigning the card.

sections.title: Creating and Checking a Token
sections.content:
The Group Owner creates a new token when the group is created and whenever its policy is updated. The token MUST be signed, using the Cryptographic Message Syntax SignedData type from RFC 3852. The content of the SignedData is the token itself, with content type id-ct-msec-token (1.3.6.1.5.5.12.1.1). The signer identifier MUST be that of the Group Owner, and the signedAttrs field MUST be present and include the signing-time attribute.

A recipient MUST check four things:

  • the signer is the expected Group Owner;
  • the signing time is newer than the one in any previously received token for that group, unless it is the first token seen;
  • the signature validates under RFC 3852;
  • the listed security and communication mechanisms (or at least one of each choice) are supported and comply with the recipient's local policy.
sections.eli5: Before trusting the card, you check that the right person signed it, that it is newer than the last card you saw, that the signature is real, and that you can actually follow the rules on it.

sections.title: The Token Structure
sections.content:
The Token is a sequence of four fields: tokenInfo, registration, rekey and data.

  • tokenInfo identifies this instance of the token: tokenDefVersion (1 for this specification), a groupName that MUST be unique relative to the Group Owner, and an optional edition number. If edition is present, entities MUST accept a token only when its value is greater than the last value seen in a valid token for that group.
  • registration lists acceptable registration and de-registration mechanisms for member-initiated joins and departures. An empty sequence means the group does not support them. The list is ordered by Group Owner preference, and a member MUST choose the highest listed mechanism its local policy supports.
  • rekey lists the rekey protocols for managing the group, with the same preference ordering rule.
  • data lists the applications used between members. A member MUST support all listed applications, and at least one mechanism where choices are given. The order of the list is the order of encapsulation.

Each protocol entry is a Protocol: an object identifier plus protocol-specific information. A GroupMngmtProtocol is either none or a supported Protocol. A LifeDate type provides timestamps and intervals as a GeneralizedTime, a UTCTime or an integer interval.

Unknown protocol identifiers MUST be handled gracefully by flagging that an unknown protocol is present. If the unknown protocol is the only allowed one in a field, the member cannot support that field and cannot join. Whether to join when an unknown protocol sits among known ones is a matter of local policy.
sections.eli5: The card has four parts: which edition of the card this is, how to join and leave, how the secret keys get refreshed, and what the group's messages should be wrapped in. Each list is in the owner's order of preference.

sections.title: Registration, Rekey and Data Policy
sections.content:
Registration. During registration a prospective member and the group controller interact so the member gets the keys and information it needs to join and take part in the group Data SA. De-registration lets a current member tell the Group Controller Key Server (GC/KS) it will stop participating. For example, the register entry might name the GSAKMP registration protocol from RFC 4535.

Rekey. During a rekey, the group can refresh or change protection keys, update the policy token and change the group membership. This field is also a sequence of protocols that the GC/KS will use.

Data. The Data SA is the ultimate consumer of the group keys. The protocols range from simple encryption or integrity use to configurable ones such as IPsec and the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (RFC 3711). Data SA mechanisms are sequenced from inside to outside: the first one defined acts on the raw data, and each later one is applied in turn.
sections.eli5: The card says how to get in and out of the club, how the club changes its secret handshake from time to time, and how to wrap messages to each other. The wrapping happens in the listed order, innermost first.

sections.title: GSAKMP and Generic Data Policies in the Appendices
sections.content:
The appendices give concrete payloads for the core token. Appendix A is the core ASN.1 module. Appendix B defines the base policy for using GSAKMP as the registration, de-registration and rekey protocol, and Appendix C defines a generic data policy.

The GSAKMP registration policy covers who may act as a GC/KS or sub-GC/KS and who may send, access control for members, the join mechanisms, and the transport. Join mechanisms can be an explicit "alaCarte" set (signature, key exchange, key wrapping, acknowledgement data and operating information) or a predefined security suite named by object identifier. The transport choice udpRTJtcpOther means the Request to Join message travels over UDP and all other group establishment messages over TCP.

The GSAKMP rekey policy covers rekey authorization, signature mechanisms, when to rekey (never, after a time, after a number of events, or a combination), the rekey method (none or GSAKMP LKH), a rekey interval, a reliability mechanism (none, resend or post) and how subordinate GC/KSes behave (none or autonomous).

The generic data policy is for applications with fixed security mechanisms. It only maps key identifiers delivered by the registration and rekey protocols to the service that uses them, for authentication and encryption, each with an optional expiration date.
sections.eli5: The back of the card has fill-in forms for the most common rules: how to prove you may join, how often to change the secret handshake, and what to do if a message about the change gets lost.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The token is only useful if recipients can verify it, so it relies on CMS digital signatures. Security therefore depends on a secure CMS implementation, a signature mechanism of appropriate strength, secure and sufficiently strong keys, and knowledge of a well-known Group Owner as the root of policy enforcement.

The Group Owner may list alternative mechanisms, but the group is only as strong as the weakest accepted mechanism. The Group Owner is responsible for listing only acceptable security mechanisms.

IANA has assigned a set of object identifiers under 1.3.6.1.5.5.12, including the token content type, security suite one, and the GSAKMP registration, de-registration and rekey protocols. Extensions in the form of objects can be registered through IANA. Extensions that change the structure of the token require an update to the tokenDefVersion field.
sections.eli5: A rule card is only as good as the person who signed it and the weakest rule on it, so the owner should only allow strong rules.

items.title: Signer
items.text: The sid in the SignerInfo is the expected Group Owner.

items.title: Freshness
items.text: The signing time is newer than in any earlier token for the group.

items.title: Mechanisms
items.text: The listed mechanisms are supported and match local policy.
